newsitem.title: GERMANY: EMU strains prompt German coalition infighting.
newsitem.headline: EMU strains prompt German coalition infighting.

text.p: Chancellor Helmut Kohl's coalition is slipping into bitter infighting as Germany strains to impose the toughest possible conditions for a European single currency that it has difficulty qualifying for itself.

At the centre of several internal disputes stands Finance Minister Theo Waigel, whose stubborn line on the planned economic and political union (EMU) worries politicians looking ahead to a series of elections next year.
In the coalition, the affable Bavarian is under pressure both to ease off and to tighten up on the Maastricht budget deficit target of three percent of gross domestic product.

The opposition Social Democrats (SPD), whose support will be needed to win parliamentary approval to join the single currency, are toying with the idea of running a Euro-sceptical campaign in the general election due in October 1998.
"We have to clear this up soon," said a strategist for Kohl's Christian Democratic Union (CDU).
"The public debate will get going later this year. If Waigel is still talking about 3.0 percent and all indications point to 3.3 or 3.4 percent, then he will look like a liar."
Waigel has quietly backed off from saying the precise "3.0 percent" and now prefers to speak only of "three percent." He insists, though, that this is not a softening of his line.

To prove this, he lashed out at Foreign Minister Klaus Kinkel this week for saying EMU's "point of no return" had been passed and that meeting the Maastricht criteria was a "process" rather than a target to be met on a certain day.
"I advise my colleague Kinkel and other European foreign ministers to stick to their own task of political union and spare us their advice about currency union," Waigel said.

Kinkel's Free Democratic Party (FDP) put this unusual attack down to nervousness within Waigel's Christian Social Union (CSU). Kinkel's spokesman Martin Erdmann responded by saying the euro was certainly a foreign ministry issue too.
That unrest in the CSU was reflected in an even tougher attack on Kinkel by Bavarian state premier Edmund Stoiber, the main rival to CSU chairman Waigel in the conservative party.
"Nobody can talk about a 'point of no return' before the numbers are known," he argued. "Anyone who does that doesn't take the stability criteria seriously."
Political analysts see Stoiber's ultra-tough line on the euro's stability as part of a Bavarian power struggle that could come to a head at the state elections next year.

Worried he might lose Euro-sceptical votes to the extreme right Republicans or to grass-roots voters' groups, Stoiber has kept up the pressure on Waigel not to budge an inch from the strictest interpretation of the Maastricht criteria.
At the same time, another party leader has urged the CSU to consider making an internal analysis of the political effect of a worst-case scenario of Germany missing the criteria.

Two CDU backbenchers touched on the same point in an open letter to fellow deputies last week accusing Waigel of focusing the EMU discussion so narrowly on the budget criteria that the larger goal of EU unity got lost.
"We have lost the political leadership and allowed the criteria to be limited to the reference values," Armin Laschet and Franz Peter Basten said in their 11-page letter.
"We must now stop falsifying this three percent into a litmus test of stable money. (The treaty) sees reaching the criteria as a process and not a 'point landing'.
"We fear we can no longer talk our way out of this in the political debate by insisting on meeting both the schedule and strict convergence as defined by this mistaken three percent interpretation."
Kohl shies away from numbers, preferring to say Bonn will meet the criteria on time and to keep up the pressure on other EU members by making clear he wants to see the project through.

"To meet his goal, Kohl needs trust and power," the Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung commented on Wednesday. "He has the former and is trying to secure the latter with his announcement that he would run for reelection again."
